title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback may herald an 'age of resentment,' top economist Steve Hanke says
excerpt: Jensen Huang return to Nvidia as CEO may fuel broader resentment toward those who appear to break the rules and get away with it, Steve Hanke said.
content_html:
By Theron Mohamed

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-27T16:04:05.050Z

Jensen Huang's stunning return to Nvidia sent investors into raptures, but it has rankled many others and could have sweeping repercussions, veteran economist Steve Hanke says.

"Thanks to the likes of Jensen Huang, I think that we are entering an age of resentment that promises a great many problems in the sphere of economic policy," Hanke told Business Insider.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on November 12 following reports that he had extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a direct report.

He was reinstated 11 days later, on November 23, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to bring him back. The news sent Nvidia stock up 31% on the day, adding nearly $1 trillion to the AI chipmaker's market capitalization, but it has since given up some of those gains.

The conduct of Silicon Valley types like Huang "flouts the moral sentiments and rules that govern and control most people's behavior," fueling public bitterness toward "this new class of big players," Hanke said.

The professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, who served on President Ronald Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, said many onlookers are indignant because they feel they've been "treated unfairly" by comparison, and have been "slighted, or abandoned, or humiliated."

In other words, they see a lack of accountability for the likes of Huang and believe they can break the rules without any lasting consequences.

A big reason for the push to bring back Huang was that he's widely considered the face of AI and integral to US success in the budding sector, given Nvidia's central role in powering and financing it.

But as the industry's champion, he also represents all that's wrong with AI in skeptics' eyes. Their concerns span from the safety of the tech to its impact on jobs to the immense resource demands of the data-center buildout.

Hanke warned that depth of resentment can be polarizing, spurring people on the right to embrace fascism, and those on the left to champion socialism.

Indeed, Americans who felt resentful of wealthy elites helped propel Trump into power in 2016, while disillusionment with wealth inequality and political corruption has fueled the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America.

"As it turns out, both the resentful on the left and the right have one thing in common: they demand that individual liberties be restricted and that the state be given more power to 'correct' things," Hanke said.

Billionaire investor and economic historian Ray Dalio has been issuing similar warnings for years.

"When broad-based discontent bubbles up and those in power allow it to grow, it can boil over to the point that when they try to put a lid on it, it explodes," he wrote in a LinkedIn post in 2024.

Moreover, veteran investor Jeremy Grantham said in 2023 that income inequality has "resulted in the estrangement, almost bitterness and anger of at least a third of the general public who feel they have been badly treated."
